tone_statements.citation: Snider, Keith. 2016. Tone in Chumburung nouns. Paper presented at the 47th Annual Conference on African Linguistics (ACAL 47), University of California, Berkeley, 23-26 March 2016. Abstract in the ACAL 47 program booklet, p.34.
tone_statements.quote: Employing autosegmental theory and an underspecification approach, I present an analysis of the tone patterns of nouns with simple stems in Chumburung [ncu], a Kwa language spoken in Ghana. CV roots have a two-way contrast: /H/ and /L/; CVV and CVN roots have four-way contrasts: /H/, /L/, /HL/, and /LH/; and, interestingly enough, CVCV roots have only three-way contrasts: /H/, /L/, and /LH/.
tone_statements.summary: H/L system; noun-root melodies /H, L, HL, LH/ with shape-dependent gaps (CV: H,L; CVCV: H,L,LH).

tone_statements.citation: Snider, Keith. 2007. Automatic and nonautomatic downstep in Chumburung: an instrumental comparison. Journal of West African Languages 34(1): 105-114.
tone_statements.quote: Chumburung has two contrastive tone levels, high tone and low tone. Unless the word ends in a glottal stop, pre-pausal low tones are always realized as low falling pitches. [...] In addition there is a lexical process of high tone spreading in which high tones, regardless of where they occur in the word, spread rightward to the right edge of the word. [...] Finally, the language has both automatic and nonautomatic downstep of high tones, which is the focus of the present work. For a more in-depth presentation of tone in Chumburung, the interested reader is referred to Snider (1986) and Chapter 4 of Snider (1999).
tone_statements.summary: 2 level tones H/L; lexical + postlexical H-spreading; floating L; automatic and nonautomatic (terracing) downstep of H, phonetically equal in size; pre-pausal L falls; no stress mentioned.

tone_statements.citation: Connell, Bruce. 2002. Tone languages and the universality of intrinsic F0: evidence from Africa. Journal of Phonetics 30(1): 101-129. doi:10.1006/jpho.2001.0156
tone_statements.quote: Chumburung (Kwa, East-Central Ghana) has two tones, H and L, and a system of nine vowels falling into two sets, /i, u, e, o/ and /ɪ, ʊ, ɛ, ɔ, a/, according to [±ATR] harmony.

sources.citation: Snider, Keith. 2007. Automatic and nonautomatic downstep in Chumburung: an instrumental comparison. Journal of West African Languages 34(1): 105-114.
sources.quote: Chumburung has two contrastive tone levels, high tone and low tone. Unless the word ends in a glottal stop, pre-pausal low tones are always realized as low falling pitches. [...] In addition there is a lexical process of high tone spreading in which high tones, regardless of where they occur in the word, spread rightward to the right edge of the word. [...] Finally, the language has both automatic and nonautomatic downstep of high tones, which is the focus of the present work. For a more in-depth presentation of tone in Chumburung, the interested reader is referred to Snider (1986) and Chapter 4 of Snider (1999).
sources.note: Section 1 'Tone in Chumburung' states the system: two contrastive tone levels H and L; pre-pausal L realized low-falling unless the word ends in a glottal stop; lexical H-tone spreading rightward to the word edge (H-falling contours phrase-finally, displaced L floats after glottal-stop words); postlexical H spreading onto the first TBU of a following L-initial word; automatic and nonautomatic (floating-L) downstep of H, cumulative/terracing, with following L also lowered. Instrumental F0 study (2 speakers, 10 tokens each) concludes both downstep types lower the register by the same amount.

sources.quote: More recently, Snider (1992) has suggested this hybrid approach as a general strategy in tone orthography, for languages in which tone bears a significant lexical load and a significant grammatical load. He illustrates this with an example from a hypothetical orthography for Chumburung (Kwa, Ghana), reproduced in Table 11. [...] Consider the two grave accents in the third phrase of Table 11. The first appears on the verb ba since this is a low tone verb even though it is pronounced with high tone as [ba] in this particular instance.
sources.locator: p. 19, section 6 'Lexical and Grammatical Marking', Table 11 'Hypothetical Tone Orthography for Chumburung (Ghana)'
sources.note: Only two mentions of Chumburung in the whole paper, both on p. 19. The passage is about orthography design, not a description of the tone system; it treats Chumburung as a language where tone carries both a significant lexical load (low-tone vs high-tone verbs; lexical tone on nouns and verbs) and a significant grammatical load (imperative marked by tone on the verb; low-tone verb ba surfaces high in the imperative frame).
